Hi Emily / Jason — thanks again for the time today. Quick recap and next steps from our discovery:

- Primary use cases you called out: (1) clinical note summarization for clinicians, (2) triage assistant for intake nurses, and (3) on-demand patient Q&A.
- Non-functional constraints: PHI-safe handling / PII redaction, deterministic stop rules for triage flows, response length ~500–1,000 tokens, and a streaming UX to let clinicians see partial answers sooner.
- Success criteria you mentioned: high precision on harms/redaction checks, <300ms first-token for short replies, and qualitatively high coherence on partial outputs (no premature truncation or weird mid-sentence stops).

Immediate next steps I promised:
1) Send recommended model variants and a short evaluation summary (attached).
2) Share the prompt-set we used for initial quality checks.
3) Dev team to follow up on streaming config and stop-sequence recommendations.
4) Align on a PoC checklist (metrics and timeline) and schedule a 30-min follow-up next week.

Attaching an initial evaluation_summary.pdf and a prompt_set_v1.jsonl (sample prompts + expected outputs). Also linking our benchmark dashboard for the few-shot tests.

Thanks — I'll follow up with model recs and an internal SRE/solutions note on streaming behavior (copying Dev & Vivek).

Hi Emily — attaching the two files I mentioned and a quick model recommendation summary below. Full benchmark dashboard is at: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/acme-health-fewshot-v1

Recommended candidates (initial):
- redwood-clinical-xl-1.0 (primary recommendation) — strong few-shot precision on medical summarization, moderate latency in batch but good streaming when configured with prefix caching.
- redwood-medium-q4_0 (cost-optimized) — lower latency, good for short Q&A flows, slightly lower long-form coherence in our tests.
- redwood-compat-small (fallback) — good when you need sub-100ms tail latency for tiny replies; expect lower overall quality for longer summaries.

Key notes:
- The evaluation_summary.pdf includes our pass/fail rates on hallucination checks and redaction tests (clinical-specific prompts). Overall the XL model had a 92% pass on redaction checks in our few-shot set; medium variant ~86%.
- Prompt set (prompt_set_v1.jsonl) includes sample system+user pairs we used for the tests, plus expected-answer snippets for automated checks.
- Streaming UX: the main issues we see in practice are (a) partial-token truncation when stop sequences are mis-specified, and (b) artifacts when the runtime flushes short chunks too aggressively. Dev will follow up with concrete runtime parameters.

Next: I'll coordinate a short PoC checklist doc (metrics + data requirements) and propose times for a 30-min sync next week. Please confirm you received the two attachments and the benchmark link.

Best,
Marissa

Subject: Re: Acme Health — streaming UX notes (technical)

Copying a few technical points for the thread so Emily / Jason have visibility. TL;DR: streaming coherence and latency trade-offs are mostly runtime/config driven — we can tune for better partial-output fluency without giving up too much latency.

Key recommendations:
1) Streaming chunk size: 64–256 token flushes depending on expected reply length. For short Q&A, prefer 64 token chunks to minimize perceived latency; for long summaries 256 reduces mid-sentence flush frequency.
2) Stop sequences: prefer explicit end-of-response tokens (e.g., "<END>") in system prompt when possible; otherwise configure the runtime to prefer "soft" stop heuristics that wait for punctuation + a brief lookahead (e.g., 8 tokens) before closing the stream. This prevents cuts like "...the patient was" -> "The"
3) First-byte latency: aim for <300ms for responses where the first emitted chunk is <64 tokens. That requires warm KV cache and small batch sizes for PoC traffic.
4) KV cache warmup: for pinned models, do a quick prefix warmup call after deploy to reduce first-request tail latency.
5) Quantization: q4_0 and q2_* reduce memory but may slightly increase token-generation jitter; for streaming prefer q4_0 on medium models and full precision for XL if you need best coherence.
6) Regression checks: add prompt-level streaming checks that compare full (non-stream) output to streamed-first-500-token concatenation and flag structural mismatches (truncated sentences, missing sections).

I can put these into a short engineering checklist we can hand to your infra team for the PoC. Happy to join the follow-up call to walk through these live and show a demo of partial streaming behavior and stop-seq configs.
